solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: French produce representative in Tom, perhaps (9)e my

indicators.note: in tells us the word for a representative sits inside the word for a tom

parts.note: a tom is a male cat, so Tom is an example of a cat
a member, as of Parliament, is an elected representative

explanation.surface: An MP or agent with the odd name Tom, perhaps, is caught up in something to do with French farm goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tom, perhaps' looks like a person's name but stands for a male cat, CAT, which wraps around MEMBER.
explanation.definitionFit: Camembert is a soft cheese made in Normandy, so it is a French dairy product.

clue.text: Bit of money I invested in fiddle

indicators.note: invested in means put inside, so I goes inside the word for fiddle

parts.note: a con is a swindle or fiddle

explanation.surface: A bit of money I put into a fraudulent scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fiddle' looks like a violin but means a swindle, CON.
explanation.definitionFit: A coin is a single metal piece of currency, a small unit of cash.

clue.text: Rub mother's herb

parts.note: Ma is mother, so mother's gives MA'S
sage is a culinary herb

explanation.surface: A rub made from mother's herbs, perhaps a home remedy.
explanation.definitionFit: A massage is a kneading of the body; to massage is to rub the muscles.

clue.text: Dirt making uniforms dirty, primarily

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so take the first letter of each of these words

explanation.surface: Dirt is what makes uniforms grubby.
explanation.definitionFit: Mud is wet earth, a common kind of grime or muck.

clue.text: Piece of primitive art, hysterically coarse

indicators.note: Piece of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An art critic denounces a crude primitive work in hysterical terms.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthy humour is crude and bawdy, so the word means coarse or vulgar.

clue.text: Quite sour nuts, greenish-blue

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters of the two words go wild and are rearranged

explanation.surface: Some rather sour nuts have a greenish-blue tinge, perhaps mouldy.
explanation.definitionFit: Turquoise is the colour of the gemstone of that name, a blue with a green cast.

clue.text: Wine studied, we hear?

indicators.note: we hear says the word for studied is to be taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: studied a subject at university means read it, past tense pronounced like the colour

explanation.surface: Someone has made a serious study of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The past tense READ is pronounced the same as the colour, which gives the wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Red is short for red wine, one of the main kinds of the drink.

clue.text: Of course, all holes circular

definitions.meaning: a ... of golf is one go at every hole of the course

explanation.surface: Of course all holes are circular, someone states the obvious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' looks like a casual 'naturally' but means of a golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: A golf round covers every hole on a course once, and round is also an adjective for circle-shaped.

clue.text: Tedious last part filling empty day

indicators.note: filling says the rear goes inside what is left of day
an empty word is left with only its outside letters, so day keeps its first and last

parts.note: the rear is the last or back part of something

explanation.surface: The final stretch of a long, empty day drags on.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreary describes something dull and depressing, which is what tedious things are.

clue.text: Popular team getting runs, one with special advantage

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
a side is a team in sport
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A popular team piles on runs and is seen as having an unfair edge.
explanation.definitionFit: An insider is someone within an organisation who has privileged knowledge or access unavailable to outsiders.

clue.text: Wake in river behind stern of steamer

indicators.note: behind says the river comes after the letter taken from steamer
the stern is the back of a ship, so stern of points to the last letter of steamer

parts.note: the Ouse is a river in England, a common crossword river

explanation.surface: A ship's wake is seen in the river behind a steamer's stern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wake' reads as a ship's trail in the water, but it is the verb meaning to stir from sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: To rouse someone is to wake them from sleep; the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Tough cut of meat — that's by the way

parts.note: hard means tough, difficult to chew
shoulder is a cut of lamb or pork

explanation.surface: A tough cut of meat is served, and the speaker adds the remark as an aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by the way' reads as a conversational aside but means beside the road. A hard shoulder is the British name for the emergency lane alongside a motorway.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard shoulder is a paved strip running alongside a motorway, literally next to the roadway.

clue.text: Wrecked, replacement of odd tyres saving vehicle, finally

indicators.note: saving here means keeping inside, so the jumbled letters hold another letter
replacement of suggests swapping things around, so these letters are rearranged
finally points to the last letter of vehicle

explanation.surface: A car was wrecked, but replacing the odd tyres saved the vehicle in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replacement of' rearranges ODDTYRES, and 'saving' makes those letters hold E, the end of vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Destroyed and wrecked both mean ruined beyond repair.

clue.text: County where people sleep

definitions.meaning: The standard abbreviation of Bedfordshire, an English county north of London

explanation.surface: A county where people sleep, as if a whole shire were a dormitory.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedfordshire is shortened to Beds in addresses, and beds are pieces of furniture for sleeping on.

clue.text: Article I encountered on the way back

indicators.note: on the way back says the word for encountered is read backwards

parts.note: met means encountered

explanation.surface: Someone describes an object they came across while returning home.
explanation.definitionFit: An item is a single thing or object in a list, the same sense as an article of clothing or merchandise.

clue.text: Remarkably ethnic, good work of art

indicators.note: remarkably suggests something unusual done to the word, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An art critic praises a remarkably ethnic and good piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remarkably' reads as praise but is the anagram signal working on the word beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An etching is a print made from an engraved metal plate, a kind of artwork.

clue.text: Cool dance music genre

parts.note: hip means fashionable or cool
a hop is an informal dance, as in a sock hop

explanation.surface: A cool dance music genre, as a club listing might put it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hip-hop is a style of popular music built on rapping over beats.

clue.text: Puzzle: was soldier Jack set up?

indicators.note: in a down clue set up means written upwards, so these letters are read in reverse

parts.note: GI is an American soldier
J is the abbreviation for jack in playing cards

explanation.surface: A puzzled question: was a soldier called Jack framed?
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' sounds like framed but reverses WASGIJ, which suits a down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A jigsaw is a picture cut into interlocking pieces to be reassembled, a classic puzzle.

clue.text: Rudeness: unfortunate recipient, men!

indicators.note: unfortunate suggests things gone wrong, so the letters of these words are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone scolds a group of men for being rude to an unlucky recipient.
explanation.definitionFit: Impertinence is cheeky lack of respect, a close synonym of rudeness.

clue.text: Gum spread round bottom of canvas

indicators.note: round says the spread goes around the letter from canvas

parts.note: pâté is a savoury spread

indicators.note: in a down clue the bottom is the last letter, here of canvas

explanation.surface: An artist spreads glue round the bottom edge of a canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spread' looks like a verb but is the noun PATE, a spreadable paste.
explanation.definitionFit: Paste is an adhesive, and gum is glue, so both are sticky substances for joining paper.

clue.text: Insect featuring in design, a termite

indicators.note: featuring in says the answer appears within these words, spanning their gaps

explanation.surface: A design shows a termite among other insects.
explanation.definitionFit: A gnat is a small flying insect, such as a midge.

clue.text: Rough-sounding canine

definitions.meaning: a ... voice is hoarse and rough
a sled dog of the Arctic

explanation.surface: A dog with a gruff bark.
explanation.definitionFit: Husky describes a hoarse voice, and it is also the name of a breed of Arctic sledge dog.

clue.text: Nothing in new design of nicest part

indicators.note: in places the round letter for nothing inside the rearranged letters
a new design rearranges things, so the letters of nicest are reordered

parts.note: O, the shape of zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: Nothing in the new design is the nicest part, a design critic's put-down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new design of' turns NICEST into SECTIN, and 'in' places O inside it before the N.
explanation.definitionFit: A section is a distinct portion or segment of a whole, so it is a part.

clue.text: Motor competition not entirely uplifting

indicators.note: in a down clue uplifting means the letters are read from bottom to top
not entirely means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a race is a speed competition

explanation.surface: Motor racing as a sport that is not altogether inspiring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not entirely' trims RACE to RAC, and 'uplifting' turns that upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Motor is an informal British word for a car.

clue.text: Pastry spoiled, odd bits removed

indicators.note: dropping the odd-numbered letters leaves the second, fourth and sixth letters of spoiled

explanation.surface: A pastry has gone off, and the bad bits are being cut away.
explanation.definitionFit: A pie is a baked dish with a pastry case, so pastry here means a pastry dish.

clue.text: Complete one sort of clue correctly

parts.note: crossword clues are either across or down, so down is one sort
right means correctly, as in answered right

explanation.surface: A solver boasts of finishing one kind of clue correctly.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue refers to itself: it is a Down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Downright as an adjective means utter or absolute, as in a downright lie, so it means complete.
